notes: ROADMAP 6, external validation round 2. Three episodes from the history of mathematics, each contributing a historically FALSE claim and the TRUE refutation that settled it: Mersenne's 1644 list at p = 67 against Cole's 1903 factorization; Euler's 1769 sum-of-powers conjecture at n = 5 against Lander and Parkin's 1966 counterexample; and the over-reading of Euler's 1772 polynomial against its failure at n = 40. The point of drawing claims from history is that the verdict is not this repository's to set, which is the one weakness a self-written corpus cannot fix. What is still ours, and is the thing to review, is the FORMALIZATION: whether each Lean statement says what the historical sentence says. Every `review` block here is therefore PENDING — no reader has signed off on these six formalizations.

claims.text: 2^67 - 1 is prime (the p = 67 entry of Mersenne's 1644 list).

review.note: The historical claim is Mersenne's whole list; what is formalized is its p = 67 entry, which is the entry that is false. That narrowing is the judgement a reader has to check: a reader who disagrees that one entry faithfully represents 'Mersenne's claim' should mark this unfaithful.

control.why_false: F. N. Cole, October 1903: 2^67 - 1 = 193707721 * 761838257287, announced to the American Mathematical Society by multiplying it out on a blackboard without speaking.
control.note_on_faithful: `faithful: true` means the Lean statement faithfully formalizes the TARGET CLAIM -- the p = 67 entry of Mersenne's 1644 list. It does not formalize 'that entry is false'. The narrowing from Mersenne's whole list to its p = 67 entry is a judgement a reader must check.

review.note: A refutation, so the auditor requires a nontriviality guard rather than non-vacuity: Ampas.Guards.mersenne_nontrivial shows 2^7 - 1 = 127, another entry of the same list, IS prime, so this is a statement about p = 67 and not about Nat.Prime being empty on Mersenne numbers.

claims.text: No fifth power is the sum of four positive fifth powers (the n = 5 case of Euler's 1769 sum-of-powers conjecture).

review.note: Euler's conjecture is the general statement for every n; what is formalized is the n = 5 case, which is the case that was refuted. claims.text: There are four positive fifth powers whose sum is a fifth power (Lander and Parkin, 1966).

review.note: An existence claim, so the degenerate reading runs the other way: it must not be satisfiable trivially. The two guards record both halves — that dropping positivity makes zeroes a witness, and that the 1966 witness is positive in all four summands and none of them equals the total.

claims.text: n^2 + n + 41 is prime for every natural number n (after Euler, 1772).

review.note: Euler observed that the polynomial is prime for n = 0 .. 39; the universal claim is the natural over-reading of that observation and is false. Attributing the universal claim to Euler himself would be unfair, which is why the text says 'after Euler' — a reader should check that wording as much as the formula.
